# Human-in-the-Loop Patterns for Research Validation

Covers where human review adds the most value in agentic research workflows, plan approval gates, source triage, claim adjudication, and the cost of human review vs automated verification.

For source details, see [citations.md](../citations.md).

## Where Human Review Adds Most Value

### Evidence from Comparative Studies

**UK Government evidence review** [17]:
- AI-assisted review: 23% faster overall (90.5 vs 117.75 hours)
- Analysis phase: 56% faster with AI
- But: AI output required more revision time (+48% more than human output; calculated from 18.25 vs 27 hours)
- Quality: Only 4 of 42 papers appeared in both AI and human reference lists
- AI excelled at individual paper summarization; struggled with cross-paper synthesis
- Key quote: "Human-only evidence reviews are already as good as they are ever going to be while AI-assisted evidence reviews are currently the worst they will ever be" [17]

**Cochrane systematic review** [18]:
- Elicit F1: 92.2%; ChatGPT F1: 89.9% (not statistically different from humans)
- Confabulation rate: 3-4% of extractions
- Recommendation: Replace second data extraction with AI; human reviewer focuses on reconciling discrepancies between human and AI extractions [18]
- Cost: Elicit $12/month, ChatGPT Plus $20/month [18]

### Highest-Value Review Points

| Review Point | Why Valuable | Evidence |
|-------------|-------------|----------|
| Plan approval | Prevents wasted effort on wrong dimensions | [16] — agents self-pause to present approaches 35% of the time |
| Source triage | Humans can assess institutional credibility that agents cannot | [17] — AI output had different literature composition |
| Cross-source synthesis | AI struggles connecting findings across papers | [17] — AI described as "an undergrad essay" |
| Claim adjudication | Final gate before claims become part of decision record | [18] — 3-4% confabulation even with high F1 |
| Footnote/implicit content | AI misses information not in prominent text positions | [17] — Claude incorrectly assessed UK coverage when info was in footnotes |

## Agent Self-Regulation

Claude Code data from Anthropic's autonomy research [16]:
- Agents self-pause more than twice as frequently as human interruptions on complex tasks
- Common triggers: present approaches (35%), gather diagnostics (21%), clarify requests (13%), request credentials (12%), seek approval (11%)
- As task complexity increases, agent-initiated stops accelerate faster than human-initiated interruptions
- This suggests well-designed agents can identify their own uncertainty boundaries

### Oversight Evolution
- New users: 20% auto-approve agent actions [16]
- Experienced users: 40%+ auto-approve [16]
- Paradoxically, interrupt rates increase with experience — indicating active monitoring rather than abdicated responsibility [16]

## Plan Approval Gates

Plan approval is the highest-leverage human intervention point in research workflows. It occurs before resource expenditure (token cost, time) and shapes all downstream work.

**What the plan should include** (derived from methodology):
- Dimensions to investigate
- File structure for outputs
- Expected data points as hypotheses
- Note that verification agents will audit the output

**Anthropic's agent teams support plan approval**: "For complex or risky tasks, you can require teammates to plan before implementing. The teammate works in read-only plan mode until the lead approves their approach" [4].

## Cost of Human Review vs Automated Verification

| Metric | Human-Only | AI-Assisted | Source |
|--------|-----------|-------------|--------|
| Total time (evidence review) | 117.75 hours | 90.5 hours (23% less) | [17] |
| Analysis phase | 34 hours | 15 hours (56% less) | [17] |
| Synthesis phase | 32.5 hours | 18.5 hours (43% less) | [17] |
| Revision phase | 18.25 hours | 27 hours (+48% more) | [17] |
| Citation audit (916 refs) | Months | 90 minutes | [6] |
| Second reviewer data extraction | Human cost | $12-20/month (Elicit/ChatGPT) | [18] |

**Key trade-off**: AI is faster at analysis but slower at revision. The net savings depend on where in the workflow AI is inserted. The largest gains come from automating the labor-intensive analysis phase while preserving human judgment for synthesis and final review [17].

## When to Ask vs Proceed Autonomously

### Agent Uncertainty Signals
Well-calibrated agents should escalate when:
- Multiple valid approaches exist (35% of Claude Code self-pauses) [16]
- Required information is unavailable (12% — credential/access requests) [16]
- The request is ambiguous (13% — clarification requests) [16]

### Autonomy Framework
Autonomy emerges from three forces: model behavior, user oversight strategy, and product design [16]. For research workflows, the key question is **reversibility**: plan changes are irreversible (they shape all subsequent work), while individual source lookups are easily revised.

**Recommendation**: Gate irreversible decisions (plan approval, dimension selection, final publication). Allow autonomous execution for reversible operations (source discovery, data extraction, draft writing).

## Gaps and Limitations

- **No study measures marginal quality improvement per additional review gate** in agentic research workflows. The cost-benefit of adding human review at each stage is qualitative, not quantitative.
- **The UK Government study** [17] is a single case study with two junior researchers — generalizing from it requires caution.
- **Cochrane study** [18] tests data extraction (structured task), not open-ended research synthesis — the confabulation rate for synthesis may be higher.
- **Trust calibration research** focuses on software development and decision support; no study addresses trust calibration specifically for citation-backed research.
- **The "transparency paradox"** (explanations can create overtrust) was reported by discovery agents but could not be verified from fetched sources.
